title: Burning Scrolls to Save Them: A New Way to Read Ancient Texts
summary: Douglas Seiler wanted to read ancient scrolls without unrolling them. He recreated the conditions of a Roman library buried by Mount Vesuvius in 79 C.E. Using papyrus, reed pens, and lampblack ink, he paid high school students to write passages from "Star Wars," the Bible, and "The Outer Limits." The experiment mimicked the catastrophe that carbonized over a thousand scrolls in Herculaneum, Italy. That eruption also buried Pompeii. The Herculaneum library is the only intact one from antiquity, possibly preserving lost works. Seiler's idea: if ancient ink contained lead, it would absorb X-rays more than the carbonized papyrus, allowing a computer to virtually flatten the scrolls and reveal the writing. In a paper published Sept. 16 in PLOS ONE, Seiler and collaborators, including Berkeley experts, report success. Even tiny amounts of lead made characters detectable with X-ray tomography. Lead absorbed up to 25 times more X-rays than the burned papyrus, making the writing stand out. "With lead in the ink, you would get a huge friggin' signature," Seiler said. "This is the Holy Grail." The team also found that a handheld X-ray fluorescence scanner could cheaply detect lead-based ink, helping identify promising scrolls for detailed imaging. So far, only a few charred scrolls have been virtually opened and deciphered, none tested for lead. A previous researcher found lead in a fragment from early physical opening attempts, which often reduced scrolls to ash. The surviving library has about 1,800 scrolls and fragments in Italy, France, and England. "Almost everything from antiquity has been destroyed," Seiler said. "But some of the Herculaneum scrolls aren't copies. These are books directly from the ancient world frozen in time." Leah Packard-Grams, a Berkeley papyrologist, said, "The stakes are the largest in the history of Greek literature."
why_it_matters: This work shows how tools borrowed from medicine and physics can recover knowledge that looked permanently lost — turning fragile, unopenable objects into readable books. It also raises systemic questions about who gets access to rare artefacts held in different countries, and which ancient voices will be recovered first when scanning time and funding are limited.

background_read: Herculaneum was a Roman town on the Bay of Naples that was buried — along with its more famous neighbour Pompeii — when Mount Vesuvius (the volcano that still overlooks Naples in Italy) erupted in 79 C.E. The scrolls come from a single luxury villa there, often called the Villa of the Papyri, whose library is thought to have belonged to a Roman statesman who was the father-in-law of Julius Caesar.

Because the eruption carbonized the scrolls instead of burning them completely, the writing is still inside them — but opening them by hand destroys them, and early attempts during the 1700s and 1800s turned many into ash. The surviving scrolls and fragments are now scattered across institutions in Italy, France and England.

In recent years the Vesuvius Challenge, an international competition, has awarded prizes to teams that use X-ray scans and machine learning to read the scrolls virtually, and researchers have recovered whole Greek words from scrolls that were never physically opened. PLOS ONE (an open-access journal where peer-reviewed science is free for anyone to read) published Seiler's experiment.
Almost all literature from antiquity has been lost, so the Herculaneum library matters because its texts may be original works rather than copies made centuries later by medieval scribes.

perspectives.description: If lead-based ink is common in the Herculaneum scrolls, the handheld scanner offers a cheap way to pick the most promising ones for expensive tomography, potentially unlocking lost plays, poems, and philosophical works. Supporters argue this is the closest thing to a time machine that classics has ever had, and it does no damage to the scrolls.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — how realistic is the test?
perspectives.description: The experiment used modern lampblack ink written on fresh papyrus, not genuine ancient ink on ancient scrolls, so the promising result may not transfer directly. The lead trace that inspired the idea came from a scroll fragment damaged during earlier physical opening attempts, which may not represent scrolls that were never opened, and no intact scroll has yet been tested for lead.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / analytical — a familiar pattern in archaeology
perspectives.description: Non-destructive imaging has repeatedly rescued texts before — CT scans of mummies, multispectral photography of reused parchment. What survives from antiquity is often a matter of accident: a library survived because it was charred rather than burned, so our picture of the ancient world is shaped by chance as much as by importance.

The logical follow-up is to screen many scrolls with the fluorescence scanner, then run full X-ray tomography on the best candidates and let software flatten and read them. If lead ink proves widespread, dozens of complete works could emerge, and scholars may need to rewrite parts of literary history — though funding, conservation rules, and international ownership questions will shape how fast that happens.
